o: There are (m−1)(n−1) total 2×2 blocks, far too many to visit individually (up to ~10¹⁰), but only ≤10⁴ black cells exist. A black cell belongs to at most 4 blocks (as top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right corner), so only blocks touching at least one black cell can have a nonzero count. Build a map from block-top-left coordinates to black-cell counts by, for each black cell, incrementing the counts of the up-to-4 candidate blocks whose corners include it (validating bounds 0 ≤ bx < m−1, 0 ≤ by < n−1). Blocks with count 0 number (m−1)(n−1) minus the number of distinct touched blocks. Both examples match: e.g., Example 2 touches 4 blocks with counts {2,2,1,1}.
k: Only blocks containing a black cell matter; each black cell influences at most 4 blocks.
arr[0] = total blocks − number of distinct blocks touched.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Map over Touched Blocks
a.i: For each black cell (x, y), loop bx ∈ {x−1, x}, by ∈ {y−1, y}; if (bx, by) is a valid block origin, increment cnt[(bx,by)]. Then fill arr from the map and compute zeros by subtraction.
s: Initialize a dictionary cnt keyed by block origins.
For each black cell, increment cnt for up to 4 in-bounds neighboring block origins.
a.t: O(k) — k = number of black cells, constant work each
a.sp: O(k) — hash map of touched blocks

a.n: Approach 2: Encode Block IDs in a Set of Pairs (Same Idea, Different Container)
a.i: Identical algorithm but encode each block origin as a single integer bx * n + by and use a plain object/array-of-counts; marginally faster constants in some languages.
s: Accumulate counts, then aggregate into arr as above.

w: Watch overflow: (m−1)(n−1) can reach ~10¹⁰, so use 64-bit integers in C++/Java. Edge cases: empty coordinates list returns [(m−1)(n−1),0,0,0,0]; black cells on the border touch fewer than 4 blocks. Follow-up: report counts for k×k blocks instead of 2×2 — same technique with more candidate offsets.
